1	\section{Method}
2	\label{sec:method}
3	
4	\subsection{Task Formulation}
5	\label{sec:task}
6	
7	Given a text $x$, we predict its \emph{generation depth} $d \in \{0, 1, 2{+}\}$: human-written ($d{=}0$), first-generation LLM output ($d{=}1$), or text produced by two or more recursive LLM generations ($d{=}2{+}$).
8	A generation chain of depth $k$ is defined recursively: $x^{(0)} \sim \mathcal{C}_0$ (human corpus), $x^{(k)} = G(x^{(k-1)})$ for $k \geq 1$, where $G$ denotes stochastic autoregressive generation.
9	Depths beyond 2 are merged into $2{+}$ because feature convergence compresses inter-class margins at deeper levels (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
10	
11	\subsection{Generation Chain Construction}
12	\label{sec:generation}
13	
14	We construct generation chains using eight generators spanning five model families: \textbf{Pythia} (2.8B, 1B) \cite{pythia}, \textbf{OLMo} (OLMo-2-1B) \cite{olmo}, \textbf{Qwen} (Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-8B-Base) \cite{qwen3}, \textbf{Llama} (Llama-3.2-3B) \cite{llama3}, and \textbf{Mistral} (Mistral-7B-v0.3) \cite{mistral7b}.
15	This selection spans parameter scales from 0.6B to 8B and diverse pretraining corpora, enabling evaluation of cross-generator and cross-scale generalization.
16	
17	For each generator, we sample approximately 1{,}000 seed passages from English Wikipedia as $\mathcal{C}_0$.
18	The same pool of seed passages serves as gen-0 for all generators.
19	We use shared seeds across generators so that cross-generator comparisons control for input content and isolate the effect of the generation model from source text variation.
20	In LOGO evaluation, gen-0 samples from the held-out generator's chains also appear (with the same text) in the training generators' chains, creating a potential train--test overlap for the gen-0 class.
21	We address this with a supplementary binary evaluation excluding gen-0 entirely (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines}).
22	Each seed is iteratively fed through the generator to produce a chain of depth 4 (i.e., gen-0 through gen-4), using the prompt ``\texttt{Continue the following text: \{text\}}''.
23	We generate up to depth~4 to empirically confirm convergence: 5-class analysis shows adjacent depths 2--4 become indistinguishable (F1\,$\approx$\,0.27; Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}), motivating the gen-2+ class collapse.
24	All generation uses temperature $\tau{=}0.7$, nucleus sampling with $p{=}0.9$, and maximum length of 256 new tokens.
25	After filtering chain breaks and passages too short for feature extraction, 37{,}058 texts remain across all depths (Appendix~\ref{app:dataset-stats}); depths 2--4 are collapsed into $2{+}$.
26	
27	\subsection{Feature Extraction}
28	\label{sec:features}
29	
30	The seven features operationalize two complementary views of distributional drift: reference-model features capture how the token-level NLL distribution shifts relative to a fixed model (location and shape statistics), while surface features capture how lexical diversity contracts under recursive generation (type-token statistics).
31	This dual-view design enables the location/shape decomposition that constitutes our primary finding.
32	We deliberately use interpretable distributional statistics so that the DDR partition remains transparent and mechanistically informative; end-to-end neural features improve classification ($+$11.6\,pp; Appendix~\ref{app:qlora}) but obscure the decomposition.
33	Cross-group ablation (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) and leave-one-feature-out analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:lofo}) confirm that both feature groups contribute independently.
34	
35	We extract seven distributional features per text (Table~\ref{tab:features}), selected to provide principled coverage of the NLL distribution---location (mean), spread (std), extremes (max, min), and tail structure (decay)---complemented by two reference-free surface diversity measures.
36	We evaluated six additional NLL statistics (median, 90th percentile, IQR, CV, skewness, kurtosis) as candidate features; all exhibit $|r| > 0.65$ with existing features and yield no classification gain when added ($\Delta$F1\,$\leq$\,$-0.011$; Appendix~\ref{app:feature-candidate}).
37

39	\centering
40	\footnotesize
41	\begin{tabular}{llp{3.8cm}}
42	\toprule
43	\textbf{Feature} & \textbf{Source} & \textbf{Measures} \\
44	\midrule
45	entropy\_mean & Ref.\ NLL & Central tendency of token surprise \\
46	entropy\_std  & Ref.\ NLL & Spread of token surprise \\
47	entropy\_max  & Ref.\ NLL & Maximum token surprise \\
48	entropy\_min  & Ref.\ NLL & Minimum token surprise \\
49	tail\_decay   & Ref.\ NLL & Log-prob decay slope (ranks 100--1K) \\
50	\midrule
51	TTR           & Surface & Type-token ratio \\
52	hapax\_ratio  & Surface & Proportion of hapax legomena \\
53	\bottomrule
54	\end{tabular}
55	\caption{Seven distributional features. Reference features use Pythia-410M per-token NLL; surface features require no reference model. DDR analysis (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) reveals that the first three drift with depth while the last four remain stable.}
56	\label{tab:features}
57	\end{table}
58	
59	\paragraph{Reference-model features.}
60	A held-out reference model (Pythia-410M, chosen to be smaller than all generators) computes per-token negative log-likelihood (NLL) for each text.
61	We use ``entropy'' as shorthand for token-level NLL throughout, following convention in prior detection work; these are point-wise NLL values, not Shannon entropy of the full distribution.
62	Although Pythia-410M shares the GPT-NeoX architecture with two of the eight generators, cross-family reference model experiments (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) confirm that depth features are not reference-specific (LOGO F1 varies by $\leq$0.013 across Pythia, OLMo, and Qwen references).
63	From the resulting NLL sequence, we extract five statistics: mean, standard deviation, maximum, and minimum of the token-level NLL, plus tail\_decay---the slope of the vocabulary-level averaged log-probability distribution in the mid-rank region (ranks 100--1000), capturing how steeply probability mass decays beyond high-frequency tokens.
64	
65	\paragraph{Surface features.}
66	Two features capture lexical diversity without requiring a reference model: type-token ratio (TTR) and the proportion of words appearing exactly once (hapax\_ratio).
67	
68	\paragraph{Feature complementarity.}
69	These features exhibit a \emph{differential depth response} (DDR), separating into drifting and non-drifting groups (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}; pairwise correlations in Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix-feature-correlation}).
70	TTR and hapax ratio are strongly correlated ($r = 0.97$); both are retained for marginal LOFO gains.
71	
72	\subsection{Evaluation Protocol}
73	\label{sec:evaluation}
74	
75	\paragraph{Cross-validation.}
76	To evaluate generalization, we use \textbf{Leave-One-Generator-Out (LOGO)} cross-validation over all eight generators.
77	LOGO holds out individual generators but does not isolate family effects; \textbf{Leave-One-Family-Out (LOFO)} addresses this by holding out entire model families (binary F1\,=\,0.686; \S\ref{sec:results-classification}).
78	Generator subsets vary across experiments (Appendix~\ref{app:gen-subsets-section}).
79	
80	\paragraph{Classifier.}
81	We use XGBoost \cite{xgboost} throughout ($n\_\text{estimators}{=}200$, $\max\_\text{depth}{=}6$, learning rate $0.1$), with identical hyperparameters across all methods in Table~\ref{tab:baselines}.
82	Alternative classifiers (CORAL \cite{coral_ordinal}, CORN \cite{corn_ordinal}, Frank-Hall \cite{frank_hall_ordinal}) yield comparable performance (Appendix~\ref{app:classifier}); discriminative power resides in the features, not the classifier.
83	
84	\paragraph{Metrics and statistical testing.}
85	The primary metric is \textbf{macro-averaged F1} over the three depth classes, with 95\% bootstrap CIs ($n{=}1{,}000$).
86	All $p$-values are two-sided with Bonferroni correction within each family of simultaneous tests.
87	
88	\paragraph{Baselines.}
89	We compare the 7-feature ensemble against four single-score detection methods repurposed as depth predictors: Avg-LogProb, FastDetectGPT \cite{fast_detectgpt}, Binoculars \cite{binoculars}, and LD-Score \cite{ld_score}.
90	Each baseline score is used as a univariate feature in the same XGBoost framework under LOGO cross-validation to ensure a controlled comparison.
91	
92	\paragraph{Length confound control.}
93	Since TTR and hapax\_ratio are mechanically length-dependent, we verify depth signal is not a length artifact via length-matched subsampling that equalizes length distributions across depth classes (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}; Appendix~\ref{app:length}).

4/3 partition stable across $|d| \in [0.10,\, 0.45]$ (silhouette\,=\,0.451).
The partition used in our analysis corresponds to the peak-silhouette region,
confirming that the drifting/stationary boundary reflects a natural gap in the
$(|\rho|, d)$ landscape rather than an artifact of a particular
threshold choice.

\paragraph{Partition stability across $\varepsilon$ thresholds.}
\label{app:epsilon-sweep}

The DDR partition classifies features as non-stationary ($d \geq \varepsilon$) or stationary ($d < \varepsilon$) based on pooled Cohen's $d$ (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
Table~\ref{tab:epsilon-sweep} reports the critical $\varepsilon$ at which each feature's classification changes; the three drifting and three near-stationary features maintain their classification for all $\varepsilon \in [0.10, 0.75]$.

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\small
\caption{Partition stability under varying $\varepsilon$. Critical threshold: the $\varepsilon$ above which a feature is reclassified as stationary. The drifting/near-stationary split is invariant for $\varepsilon \in [0.10, 0.75]$; only entropy std ($d{=}0.55$) changes at $\varepsilon > 0.55$.}
\label{tab:epsilon-sweep}
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{llcc}
\toprule
\textbf{DDR Zone} & \textbf{Feature} & \textbf{Pooled $d$} & \textbf{Stationary at $\varepsilon >$} \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Drifting} & $\bar{H}$ (ent.\ mean) & 1.17 & 1.17 \\
 & TTR & 0.88 & 0.88 \\
 & hapax ratio & 0.76 & 0.76 \\
\midrule
Intermediate & $\sigma_H$ (ent.\ std) & 0.55 & 0.55 \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Near-stat.} & $H_{\max}$ (ent.\ max) & 0.08 & 0.08 \\
 & tail decay & 0.08 & 0.08 \\
 & $H_{\min}$ (ent.\ min) & 0.016 & 0.016 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

\noindent The 3/1/3 partition is stable across $\varepsilon \in [0.10, 0.75]$: the three drifting features remain non-stationary at all $\varepsilon < 0.76$, the three near-stationary features remain stationary at all $\varepsilon > 0.08$, and only entropy std changes classification (becoming stationary at $\varepsilon > 0.55$), confirming it as the sole threshold-sensitive feature.
The minimum gap between adjacent zone boundaries ($d_{\text{hapax}} - d_{\sigma_H} = 0.21$) exceeds typical effect-size estimation uncertainty, providing a margin against sampling noise.

\subsection*{Holdout Generator Split Validation}
\label{app:holdout-split}

To confirm the DDR partition is not an artifact of the specific generator pool, we split the eight generators into disjoint selection (4) and validation (4) sets, compute per-subset pooled $(|\rho|, d)$, and check whether all seven features receive the same zone assignment in both subsets.
We evaluate two complementary splits to avoid dependence on a single partition:
Split~A selects \{Pythia-2.8B, Qwen3-1.7B, OLMo, Mistral\} (validation: Pythia-1B, Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-8B, Llama);
Split~B selects \{Pythia-1B, Qwen3-0.6B, OLMo, Mistral\} (validation: Pythia-2.8B, Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-8B, Llama).

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\small
\caption{Holdout split validation of the DDR partition. Selection (sel) and validation (val) $|\rho|$ and $d$ for two disjoint 4/4 generator splits. Zone assignment is identical across all four subsets for every feature.}
\label{tab:holdout-split}
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{llcccccc}
\toprule
& & \multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{Split A}} & \multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{Split B}} \\
\cmidrule(lr){3-5} \cmidrule(lr){6-8}
\textbf{Zone} & \textbf{Feature} & sel $|\rho|$ & val $|\rho|$ & $\Delta|\rho|$ & sel $|\rho|$ & val $|\rho|$ & $\Delta|\rho|$ \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Drifting} & $\bar{H}$ (ent.\ mean) & 0.60 & 0.58 & 0.02 & 0.60 & 0.58 & 0.02 \\
 & TTR & 0.61 & 0.59 & 0.02 & 0.60 & 0.59 & 0.01 \\
 & hapax ratio & 0.62 & 0.60 & 0.02 & 0.62 & 0.61 & 0.01 \\
\midrule
Intermediate & $\sigma_H$ (ent.\ std) & 0.19 & 0.21 & 0.02 & 0.22 & 0.17 & 0.05 \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Near-stat.} & $H_{\min}$ (ent.\ min) & 0.39 & 0.36 & 0.03 & 0.38 & 0.37 & 0.01 \\
 & $H_{\max}$ (ent.\ max) & 0.05 & 0.05 & 0.00 & 0.04 & 0.06 & 0.02 \\
 & tail decay & 0.10 & 0.08 & 0.02 & 0.11 & 0.07 & 0.04 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

Under simple joint $(|\rho|, d)$ thresholds, both splits produce a 3/2/2 partition: entropy min is classified as a second intermediate feature due to its elevated pooled $|\rho|$ (0.36--0.39).
However, entropy min's binary (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+) $d$ values are uniformly below 0.06 across all four split${\times}$subset combinations, consistent with near-stationarity on the task-relevant metric; its pooled $|\rho|$ reflects change concentrated at the gen-0/gen-1 boundary rather than sustained drift.
Five of seven features are unambiguously classified under any reasonable criterion; entropy min's boundary status is resolved by the binary-task $d$ criterion.

Selection and validation subsets produce identical partitions in both splits (Table~\ref{tab:holdout-split}; Figure~\ref{fig:holdout-scatter}).
The maximum $\Delta|\rho|$ between selection and validation is 0.05 (entropy std, Split~B), and the minimum gap between adjacent zones remains $>$0.15 in all subsets.

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig_ddr_holdout_split.pdf}
\caption{Holdout split validation in $(|\rho|, d)$ space. Filled markers: selection set; hollow: validation set. Zone assignments are identical across subsets; selection/validation pairs cluster tightly for all features.}
\label{fig:holdout-scatter}
\end{figure}

\subsection*{Heteroscedasticity Sensitivity}
\label{app:heteroscedasticity}

Levene tests reject equal variance between gen-1 and gen-2+ for drifting features ($p < 10^{-10}$; variance ratios 1.86--2.21).
To verify that the DDR partition is robust to this heteroscedasticity, we supplement pooled Cohen's $d$ with Glass's $\Delta$ (using the gen-1 standard deviation as denominator) and Cliff's $\delta$ (a non-parametric ordinal effect size; Table~\ref{tab:effect-sizes}).

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\small
\caption{Effect size comparison (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+, $N$\,=\,29{,}095). Glass's $\Delta$ uses the gen-1 SD as denominator; Cliff's $\delta$ thresholds follow Romano et al.\ (2006): $|\delta| < 0.147$ negligible, $< 0.33$ small, $< 0.474$ medium, otherwise large.}
\label{tab:effect-sizes}
\begin{tabular}{llrrr}
\toprule
\textbf{Zone} & \textbf{Feature} & \textbf{$|d|$} & \textbf{$|\Delta|$} & \textbf{$|\delta|$} \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Drifting} & ent.\ mean & 1.054 & 1.410 & 0.587 \\
 & TTR & 0.814 & 1.116 & 0.510 \\
 & hapax ratio & 0.735 & 0.936 & 0.528 \\
\midrule
Intermediate & ent.\ std & 0.457 & 0.605 & 0.295 \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Near-stat.} & tail decay & 0.087 & 0.099 & 0.072 \\
 & ent.\ max & 0.062 & 0.065 & 0.021 \\
 & ent.\ min & 0.016 & 0.015 & 0.354$^{\dagger}$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\noindent Effect sizes in Table~\ref{tab:effect-sizes} are computed on the binary task (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+); the main text (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) reports 3-class pooled $d$ values (e.g., hapax ratio $d{=}0.76$), which are slightly larger because the gen-0/gen-1 contrast contributes additional separation.
Glass's $\Delta$ amplifies drifting effects (1.41 vs.\ 1.05 for entropy mean) because gen-2+ variance exceeds gen-1 variance (ratio 2.08), making the pooled Cohen's $d$ conservative.
Near-stationary features remain negligible under both parametric metrics ($|\Delta| \leq 0.099$).
The minimum drifting-to-maximum-near-stationary gap is $9.5\times$ under Glass's $\Delta$ (0.936\,/\,0.099); heteroscedasticity does not erode the partition.
Cliff's $\delta$ classifies all drifting features as ``large'' ($|\delta| > 0.474$) and entropy std as ``small'' ($|\delta|{=}0.295$), consistent with the parametric partition.

\noindent $^{\dagger}$Entropy min's elevated Cliff's $\delta$ (0.354, ``medium'') reflects distributional shape asymmetry between gen-1 and gen-2+ that rank-based statistics detect but location measures do not (Cohen's $d{=}0.016$, Glass's $\Delta{=}0.015$).
This is consistent with its documented boundary status (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}): the gen-0/gen-1 transition produces rank-order shifts that persist into deeper generations without affecting the mean.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

Recursive generation alters \emph{where} the token-level surprise distribution sits but not \emph{how} it is shaped---a dichotomy with a mechanistic basis.
Under nucleus sampling, top-$p$ truncation preserves the functional form of the conditional distribution at each step; what changes is the \emph{input}: as the model conditions on increasingly self-typical outputs, expected NLL compresses monotonically.
This yields two testable predictions: (1)~increasing sampling randomness should weaken the location drift, and (2)~semantic-preservation constraints should attenuate it.
Both are confirmed: at $t{=}1.0$, location signal collapses ($\rho$: $-0.60 \to -0.002$; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}); under elaboration prompts, drift weakens (F1\,=\,0.730 vs.\ 0.781; Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}).
Causal analyses corroborate: drifting features contribute $5.5\times$ more to classification, with 6/7 exhibiting significant Granger causality over the five-point chain (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-causality}).
Intuitively, top-$p$ truncation restricts token selection but preserves the conditional distribution's functional form; shape statistics are thus inherited from pretrained weights, while entropy std ($d{=}0.55$) shows intermediate behavior as a second-order location effect ($\text{Var} = E[X^2] - E[X]^2$ responds to mean shift even when shape is preserved).
These results are established under nucleus sampling ($p{=}0.95$); at $\tau{=}1.0$---where truncation is near-minimal---shape features remain stable ($d < 0.15$; Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-temp-stability}), but verification under non-autoregressive decoding strategies remains open.

The classifier is a proof-of-concept for corpus-level auditing, not per-document filtering: gen-1 per-class F1\,=\,0.63 is insufficient for individual flagging but supports batch-level contamination estimation (${\pm}3$--$4$\% at $n{=}1{,}000$; Appendix~\ref{app:error-analysis}).
Depth-aware filtering can serve as a prophylactic against model collapse \cite{drayson_detection_prevents_collapse}, though depth-stratified curation does not yet improve downstream training (TOST equivalence at $\varepsilon{=}{\pm}2\%$; Appendix~\ref{app:downstream})---consistent with depth compressing surface statistics rather than the semantic content driving task performance; the primary value lies in provenance, not training improvement.

DDR is mechanistically distinct from model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse}: retraining erodes tail coverage by updating weights, whereas inference-chain drift at fixed parameters shifts only location, leaving shape stable.
Vocabulary impoverishment alone cannot explain this asymmetry: if depth simplified the lexicon, shape features should also compress, yet they remain stable ($d < 0.10$; \S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
Prior work documents \emph{what converges}---diversity loss \cite{curious_decline}, attractor dynamics \cite{markovian_chains}---but not what is \emph{preserved}; this complementary observation enables depth detection without per-generator calibration.
The decomposition itself---identifying which distributional properties carry cross-generator depth signal---constitutes the analytical contribution, independent of whether shape stability originates from sampling truncation or deeper autoregressive properties.
Three depth classes represent the practical resolution ceiling (5-class F1\,$\approx$\,0.50; Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}); QLoRA recovers more signal (F1\,=\,0.905, 6-gen LOGO; Appendix~\ref{app:qlora}), reflecting token-order patterns that aggregate statistics miss.
Instruction-tuned models substantially compress DDR structure (silhouette 0.660$\to$0.372; entropy-mean $\rho$ reverses sign; 3-class F1 degrades 3.7--19.9\,pp), with model-dependent heterogeneity ruling out a uniform mechanism (Appendix~\ref{app:instruct}).
Yet QLoRA recovers to 0.89--0.91 on instruct data, confirming that depth signal persists at the token-sequence level beyond DDR's summary-statistic decomposition.
Cross-domain evaluation (News, Academic, Code; $t{=}1.0$) yields binary F1\,=\,0.74--0.75 but degraded 3-class F1 (0.62--0.65; Appendix~\ref{app:domain}), with temperature and domain effects confounded.
Our generation chains use open-ended continuation prompts; real-world recursive pipelines---instruction-following chains, multi-turn dialogues, mixed-model editing---may attenuate, restructure, or introduce confounds not present in controlled chains.

Entropy std (wine; $d{=}0.55$) is an intermediate member; non-drifting features (amber; $d < 0.10$) show negligible drift. 71	\end{figure}
```
72	
73	Pooled class-balanced Spearman correlations with depth confirm the binary split (Figure~\ref{fig:feature-drift}):
74	drifting features show substantial monotonic trends (hapax ratio $\rho = -0.64$, TTR $\rho = -0.63$, entropy mean $\rho = -0.60$),
75	while non-drifting features remain near-zero (tail decay $|\rho| = 0.04$; per-depth distributions in Appendix~\ref{app:feature-distributions}).
76	The six-fold magnitude gap between drifting ($|\rho| > 0.60$) and non-drifting features ($|\rho| \leq 0.16$) defines the DDR partition.
77	Within the non-drifting group, entropy std ($|\rho| = 0.16$, $d{=}0.55$) shows a substantial level shift despite low monotonicity, distinguishing it from the three near-stationary features ($d < 0.10$); this refinement is stable across $d$ thresholds in $[0.56, 0.75]$ (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}).

79	\paragraph{Quantification.}
80	Convergence across parametric and non-parametric effect-size measures confirm the split.
81	Cohen's $d$ \cite{cohen1988statistical} shows a ${\geq}7\times$ gap between drifting ($d{=}0.76$--$1.17$) and near-stationary features ($d \leq 0.08$); KS statistics, Glass's $\Delta$, Cliff's $\delta$, and CV shift all corroborate (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}).
82	Four features fall cleanly into drifting or non-drifting groups.
83	Entropy min and tail decay are \emph{boundary features}: entropy min is near-stationary for gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+ ($d{=}0.016$) but sensitive at gen-0/gen-1 ($|\rho|{=}0.40$); tail decay passes TOST for only 4/8 generators ($|d|{=}0.10$--$0.22$).

85	\paragraph{Validation.}

90	Reclassifying either boundary feature as intermediate preserves the core drifting/non-drifting split and leaves classification unchanged.
91

107

1	\section{Related Work}
2	\label{sec:related}
3	
4	\subsection{AI-Generated Text Detection}
5	\label{sec:related-detection}
6	
7	The detection literature spans statistical tests \cite{gltr,grover,release_strategies}, zero-shot scoring \cite{detectgpt,fast_detectgpt,binoculars,dna_gpt}, surprisal diversity \cite{diveye}, geometric invariants \cite{intrinsic_dim_detection}, and learned classifiers \cite{ghostbuster,feat_aug_transformer,reliable_detection,ld_score}; see \citet{wu_survey_2025} and \citet{jawahar_survey} for surveys.
8	RAID \cite{raid} benchmarks binary detection across generators and attacks; we extend the task from binary to ordinal depth estimation.
9	Several recent efforts move beyond the binary boundary---collaboration roles \cite{beyond_binary}, joint detection-attribution \cite{two_birds}, creator-editor modes \cite{beyond_final_actor}, multi-generator attribution \cite{semeval2024_task8}---but all taxonomize by \emph{source} or \emph{production mode}, not recursive generation \emph{depth}; repurposing their scores as depth predictors reveals high cross-generator variance (binary F1\,=\,0.52--0.71; Table~\ref{tab:baselines}) \cite{paraphrase_evades,detection_possibilities}.
10	Our contribution is orthogonal: ordinal depth classification \cite{gutierrez_ordinal_survey,coral_ordinal,kasa_ordinality_nlp} as a task, and the finding that combining drifting and stationary features yields consistent cross-generator performance where individual detection scores show high variance \cite{uchendu_attribution,munir_looking_glass}.
11	
12	\subsection{Model Collapse and Iterative Generation}
13	\label{sec:related-collapse}
14	
15	Self-consuming generative models progressively lose distributional coverage \cite{self_consuming_mad,curse_of_recursion,seddik_synthetic_data}, though data mixing mitigates collapse \cite{model_collapse_avoidable,strong_model_collapse}.
16	These studies address \emph{training-loop} degradation where parameter updates erode tail coverage; indeed, \citet{schaeffer_collapse_position} identify eight distinct definitions of ``collapse,'' most tied to retraining dynamics.
17	We study \emph{inference chains} where parameters are fixed and only the input distribution evolves.
18	Two concurrent works are most directly relevant: \citet{broken_telephone} analyze paraphrasing and translation chains, documenting progressive information loss, while \citet{markovian_chains} demonstrate attractor dynamics that bound distinguishable depth to approximately three classes; \citet{attractor_cycles} provide complementary evidence that LLM outputs converge to cyclic attractor states under repeated generation.
19	We study \emph{non-paraphrastic continuation} chains, where the absence of semantic anchoring permits richer depth signal, and offer a complementary decomposition: where these works characterize \emph{that} and \emph{why} convergence occurs, DDR isolates \emph{what} converges (NLL location) from what is preserved (NLL shape), enabling ordinal classification without per-generator calibration.
20	The independent convergence of all three approaches on ${\sim}$3 distinguishable depth classes---via Markovian dynamics \cite{markovian_chains}, information-theoretic loss \cite{broken_telephone}, and distributional feature compression (this work)---points to a shared resolution ceiling in recursive text generation (Table~\ref{tab:iterative-comparison} in Appendix~\ref{app:iterative-comparison} provides a structured comparison).
21	
22	\subsection{Vocabulary Diversity and Stylometry}
23	\label{sec:related-diversity}
24	
25	Declining lexical diversity in LLM text is documented in both training \cite{curious_decline} and deployment settings \cite{writing_diversity}; MAUVE \cite{mauve} provides a divergence-based metric for quantifying this distributional gap.
26	Our surface features (TTR, hapax ratio) are classical stylometric measures \cite{stamatatos_survey,koppel_authorship}; we repurpose them from generator identity \cite{uchendu_attribution} to the depth dimension, where their monotonic decline under top-$p$ sampling \cite{nucleus_sampling} constitutes a drifting component of DDR.
27	
28	\subsection{Data Quality and Provenance}
29	\label{sec:related-provenance}
30	
31	Scalable data curation relies on quality signals \cite{dsir,qurating,ccnet}; generation depth offers a complementary provenance axis.
32	Proactive watermarking \cite{watermark_llm,synthid_text,aaronson_watermark} embeds identifiable patterns but degrades across multi-step chains \cite{chainwash}, motivating passive approaches.
33	Our NLL-based analysis connects to \citet{min_k_percent} (probability-tail membership inference) but extends from binary membership to full distributional decomposition for ordinal depth.
34	\citet{koike_mia_detection} formalize this connection from the opposite direction, showing that detection scores implicitly perform membership inference, underscoring the shared statistical basis of detection and provenance.
```

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

AI text detection asks a single binary question---\emph{human or machine?}---and recent methods answer it with increasing reliability \cite{detectgpt,fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score}.
Yet this framing elides a richer structure emerging on the open web: as LLM outputs re-enter training corpora \cite{dolma,fineweb} and seed further generation, text accumulates at varying \emph{recursive depths}---an estimated 7--17\% of recent scientific publications already contain substantial LLM-modified content \cite{mapping_llm_science,monitoring_ai_review}---and each generation cycle pushes distributional properties further from both the human source and the first-generation predecessor.


```

Now I'm moving into the core problem: while most deployed systems use instruction-tuned models, the base models are what matter for synthetic data and recursive augmentation, so that's where I'm focusing. The key insight is that knowing the generation depth matters for understanding data provenance and model collapse, but existing methods only give us a binary answer. Distributional compression happens predictably across recursive generations, so I'm proposing depth fingerprinting to classify text by how many times it's been recursively generated rather than just whether it's human or machine.

Testing this across eight different base models of varying sizes and architectures, I'm finding something interesting: the central tendency of the distribution—things like mean entropy and lexical diversity—shifts consistently as generation depth increases, but the shape of the distribution—the extremes and tail behavior—stays remarkably stable. This differential depth response appears to be a fundamental property of how autoregressive sampling works, distinct from the kind of tail erosion you see in model collapse.
```

\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

All eight generators are base (pretrained) models; instruction-tuned variants show substantially degraded depth signal (Appendix~\ref{app:instruct}), and extending the method to RLHF-aligned models---which dominate real-world text---requires addressing confounds from length regulation and safety-driven distribution shaping.
Our largest generator is 8.2B parameters; frontier models (70B+) remain untested and their higher fluency may further compress feature margins.

The evaluation assumes a fixed decoding regime (temperature 0.7, nucleus $p{=}0.9$); cross-temperature transfer degrades when test-time temperature exceeds training-time settings (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-temp}).
All seed texts are English Wikipedia excerpts, and the reference model (Pythia-410M) has English-centric pretraining, limiting non-English applicability.

Depth resolution is bounded at three classes (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+); finer-grained classification (5-class) yields F1\,$\approx$\,0.50 with depths 2--4 mutually indistinguishable (Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}).
Finally, our cross-model chain and simulated editing experiments (\S\ref{sec:discussion}) represent controlled laboratory settings; the gap to real-world post-processing pipelines remains untested.
